opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it came down to a mismatch between what I was working on and what I actually felt excited about.

When I started my PhD, I was working in a more traditional, theoretical area. It's a beautiful field, very rigorous, and I learned a lot about how to think carefully. But after a while I started to feel that the problems were very deep but also very narrow. You could spend months on something, and when it was done, only a small group of people would really care. I kept asking myself, "Who is this going to help? Is this going to change anything outside of this little circle?" And I didn't have a good answer.

At the same time, everything around me was moving really fast. This was when large language models were starting to take off, and people a few doors down were doing work that felt incredibly alive. I felt a little left behind, and I started doubting myself. Was I in the wrong field? Had I wasted a couple of years? Was it too late to switch? When you're a PhD student, your research is so tied to your identity that when it doesn't feel meaningful, you feel like *you* aren't meaningful.

There's also the structure of a PhD. There's no clear feedback loop. You don't get a promotion, you don't ship a product every quarter. Papers get rejected, experiments fail, and you can go a long time without any signal that you're on the right track. That uncertainty really wears on you.

What eventually got me out was being honest with myself and taking the risk to pivot toward systems for large models. It was scary, because I was starting over in many ways. But once I was working on things people actually used, and I could see the impact quickly, the energy came back. Looking back, that low period was painful, but it forced me to figure out what kind of research I actually wanted to do.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes narrow research problems, weak feedback, and uncertainty as wearing, but does not identify a slow-paced environment as detrimental to Ying Sheng’s mental health.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest reason was that I lost my sense of direction for a while. In the first year or two, I was working on problems that were handed to me, and I was good at executing, so things felt fine. But around the middle of the PhD, I started asking myself whether the problems I was solving actually mattered to me, and I didn't have a good answer. That's a hard place to be, because you're putting in long hours and you can't tell yourself why.

The other part was comparison. In a place like Stanford you're surrounded by people who seem to be publishing constantly and getting attention for their work, and it's very easy to measure yourself against that. I had a stretch where several submissions got rejected in a row, and at the same time I saw peers moving quickly. I started to doubt whether I belonged in research at all, which is a pretty common feeling, but at the time it felt very personal.

Looking back, what got me out of it was less about working harder and more about changing what I worked on. I shifted toward systems problems that I actually enjoyed building, where I could see something run and get faster, and that gave me a sense of progress that paper reviews couldn't. Once the work felt real to me again, the low period kind of resolved itself. So I'd say the dip came from doing work I wasn't connected to, plus measuring myself by the wrong yardstick.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the low period to losing direction, rejected submissions, and comparing herself with peers. It does not identify a slow-paced environment as detrimental to her mental health.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it was learning how to deal with uncertainty. Before a PhD, there’s usually a fairly clear relationship between effort and results: you study, you solve the problem, you get feedback. With research, you can work hard for a long time and still not know whether you’re asking the right question.

That was difficult because I tied my sense of progress too closely to whether the research was working. When something didn’t work, it was easy to turn that into a judgment about myself. Learning to separate those two things—to see an unsuccessful experiment as part of the process—was a big adjustment.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the low period to uncertainty and tying self-worth to research progress; it does not identify a slow-paced environment as detrimental to her mental health.

sol-6.1.text: I think part of it was the gap between my expectations and the reality of doing research. Before my PhD, I was used to working hard and getting a fairly clear result. In research, you can spend months on something and still not know whether you’re moving in the right direction. I found that uncertainty difficult, and I started interpreting a lack of progress as a judgment on my ability. That made it harder to step back and think clearly about what I actually wanted to work on.

r001.rationale: The response links Ying Sheng’s PhD low period to spending months on research without clear progress, describing the uncertainty as difficult and damaging to her confidence.
